purpose: Tests whether Voynich "entities" (word cores, after stripping hand-picked prefixes/suffixes) occupy a low-rank attribute space forming a few coherent declension classes that map onto sections and label-vs-prose, plus whether folio-opener cores form an index-like sequence — taken together as evidence of a real inflectional/indexed language.
soundness_reason: Multiple confounds and circularity, no nulls. (1) section() uses hand-rolled folio-number ranges (herbal<=66, etc.) instead of the real IVTFF 'I' labels in C['meta'] — the documented mismatch confound. (2) No Currier A/B control: cluster-to-section associations could simply track the A/B dialect split rather than "declension class," yet A/B is never read. (3) The "low rank => few declension TYPES" claim is circular and confound-#5/#6 territory: PRE/SUF are an analyst-chosen affix inventory, so normalized affix profiles are guaranteed to live in a few-dimensional simplex, and a content-free productive-morphology generator reproduces exactly this low-rank paradigmatic structure — no content-free null is run, so low-rank cannot be read as meaning. (4) The "JOIN" cross-modal test is effectively void: at lab/tot>0.3 with freq>=12, it finds 0 label-entities, so the headline label-vs-prose result is null/non-informative; the prose section mix shown (recipes .35, herbal .27) just mirrors section size (confound #2). (5) The "depth axis" index claim (74% unique opener cores => "index-like") has no null — an open lexicon (high hapax/Heaps, confound #6) makes first-words-of-paragraphs mostly distinct in any productive vocabulary, so distinctness does not discriminate an index from ordinary open-vocabulary text. Conclusions overreach every test.
value_reason: The mechanics (affix-profile PCA + k-means on cores) are a legitimate descriptive exercise, but as written it contributes no discriminating test: it lacks a content-free null, ignores A/B, uses fake folio-range sections, and its cross-modal "join" returns an empty set. Every interpretive label (declension TYPES, the JOIN, index-like depth axis) is decorative narrative unsupported by a control, redundant with already-confounded section/morphology work.
reusable_test: Clustering word-cores by normalized affix-distribution profiles and checking the rank/dimensionality of that space CAN be a useful morphological-class probe — but only as a discriminating test if run identically on a content-free productive-morphology generator and on a known inflected natural language, with the real-corpus low-rank/cluster-purity compared against those baselines (and with section labels taken from real IVTFF 'I' metadata and Currier A/B held fixed).

no Currier A/B dialect control
no content-free / productive-morphology null for low-rank and clustering
section-size drives prose section mix
open-lexicon trivially makes opener cores distinct (no index null)

key_result: 191 cores (freq>=12, 85% of tokens); affix-profile space is low-rank (top-3 comps 66%, top-6 81% variance); k-means yields 6 lopsided classes (sizes 62/5/16/59/1/48) whose top section just tracks the largest sections (recipes/herbal); the label-vs-prose JOIN finds 0 label-entities (null result); 74% of folio-opener cores are unique, declared "index-like" with no null.

purpose: Tests whether the manuscript's section structure can be recovered from page IMAGES alone (ink coverage, green/red-brown/blue pigment fractions, stroke edge-density as "text-likeness"), with no text or metadata, by auto-labeling each PDF page with a hand-tuned visual taxonomy.
soundness_reason: The feature-extraction mechanic is legitimate and, importantly, operates in a modality fully INDEPENDENT of every text-based confound (no lexicon, no A/B dialect, no shared-vocab size effects, no content-free-generator issue). That independence is the script's real virtue. But the segmentation step is unvalidated: label() is a stack of magic-number thresholds (green>0.05, edge>=1.2, etc.) with NO comparison to the ground-truth IVTFF 'I' labels that sit in corpus.json['meta'], no confusion matrix, no accuracy figure, and no null/baseline. When run, it dumps 119/209 pages (57%) into a catch-all "mixed" bucket, recovers only HERBAL (85) and a mere 5 scattered TEXT-DENSE pages, and entirely fails to surface the real biological/balneo (blue baths), zodiac, astronomical, cosmological, pharma, and the contiguous recipes/stars text section. So it does NOT actually "recover the section structure" as the docstring claims. Additional flaws: it conflates PDF page index with folio (each folio spans multiple recto/verso/foldout pages), and the 256x355 downscale degrades the very stroke detail its edge metric depends on. Valid mechanic, conclusion ("recovered structure") overreaches the result.
value_reason: As written it performs no discriminating test: it never scores its visual labels against the real 'I' labels available in the corpus, never reports accuracy, and has no null. The output is a noisy run-length narrative dominated by a 57% "mixed" blob, so it neither cleanly measures real structure nor distinguishes meaningful from content-free. The underlying idea (an image-domain cross-check independent of text confounds) is genuinely worthwhile but is not realized here, so this instance is decorative rather than discriminating.
reusable_test: Derive page-type purely from independent image features (pigment/ink/stroke-edge density) and score it against the ground-truth IVTFF 'I' section labels via a confusion matrix; agreement above a label-shuffled null would validate the section taxonomy without circular reliance on the transcription. (This script gestures at the test but omits the scoring/null.)

No null/baseline or accuracy metric for the heuristic labels
PDF page index conflated with folio (recto/verso/foldouts span multiple pages)
Hand-tuned threshold constants with no calibration

Dominant 'mixed' bucket (57%) treated as a result rather than a failure to segment
key_result: Runs successfully on Voynich_Manuscript.pdf. Outputs a run-length page segmentation and summary {'mixed': 119, 'HERBAL (foliage+roots)': 85, 'TEXT-DENSE (recipes/stars)': 5}. It recovers a herbal-dominant signal but collapses most of the manuscript (57%) into "mixed" and misses the biological/zodiac/astro/cosmo/pharma and recipes-text sections, so it does not actually recover the section structure.

purpose: Claims to recover the manuscript's "library architecture" — a catalog of source works, a cross-reference network among them, a shared lingua-franca stratum, and a hub/isolated functional map — from morphological "core" vocabulary shared across sections.
soundness_reason: Hits four established confounds at once. (1) Sections are hand-rolled folio-number ranges (n<=66 herbal, etc.) while the real IVTFF 'I' labels sit unused in meta — the "pharma" range is known to mismatch actual herbal pages (confound #1). (2) The cross-reference matrix is a normalized enrichment obs/(len(A)*len(B)/U), which the session proved inflates for the SMALLEST sections (confound #4); the output confirms this exactly — the two crowned "hubs" by mean enrichment are cosmo (1,616 tok) and astro (1,020 tok), the two tiniest sections, while the two largest (herbal, recipes) rank lowest. The "hub" conclusion is a small-denominator artifact, not integration. (3) No Currier A/B control: cross-section overlap tracks the documented dialect split, not "function" (confound #3). (4) No permutation/significance null on the enrichment ratios — it just declares >1 a "real cross-reference." Additionally the "entities" are content-free morphological stems (the shared stratum even includes the empty string ''), which a productive content-free generator reproduces (confound #5), so the whole "catalog of source-works / lingua franca" framing is unsupported interpretation layered on confounded numbers.
value_reason: Pure interpretive narrative ("library's shadow", "lingua franca", "compiler's invariant vocabulary", hub/isolated map) built on confounded section ranges, a small-denominator enrichment ranking, and content-free stems. It contributes no discriminating test that separates meaningful from content-free structure; its strongest "finding" (cosmo/astro hubs) is a known artifact and is contradicted by section size.
reusable_test: none

small-denominator inflation of normalized enrichment (smallest sections crowned as hubs)
Currier A/B dialect split driving cross-section overlap
no permutation/size null for enrichment significance
content-free morphological stems treated as semantic entities
key_result: Outputs a 6-section catalog and an enrichment matrix that ranks the two SMALLEST sections (cosmo 2.32, astro 2.15) as the top integration hubs and the two LARGEST (recipes 1.25, herbal 1.17) as least connected — a textbook small-denominator artifact — plus a "shared stratum" of 94 multi-work stems that even includes the empty string. No null, no A/B control, real section labels ignored.

purpose: Tests whether Voynichese line types defined by their REAL IVTFF locus tag (P=prose, L=label, C=circular, R=radial) differ statistically — word length, adjacent repetition, vocabulary overlap, and word-initial glyph distribution — as a real language's picture-labels vs running prose would, plus measures the line-initial gallows enrichment.
soundness_reason: Strengths: it uses the REAL locus-tag line types (not hand-rolled folio ranges), so confound #1 is avoided, and the paragraph-initial anomaly is measured against a proper within-corpus baseline (line-initial% vs mid-line%), yielding a clean genuine structural finding (p x17.5, t x5.3, y x4.4 line-initial). The label-vs-prose novelty claim ("54% of label vocab never seen in prose") is printed as a raw fraction with NO null, and given the corpus's ~72%-hapax open lexicon this looks like a small-denominator/open-lexicon artifact — yet a size-matched permutation null I ran shows an equal-sized random prose draw yields only ~1% novelty vs labels' 54%, so the effect is in fact real (the script just fails to demonstrate it). Weakness: the label-novelty and start-glyph differences are not controlled for Currier A/B dialect or for which sections labels concentrate in (confound #3), and adj-rep% trivially tracks line length (labels avg 1.18 words/line so near-zero adjacency is mechanical, not 'less repetitive'). The script mostly reports numbers without overclaiming meaning, but its docstring frames the result as a real-language signature.
value_reason: The line-initial vs mid-line glyph-enrichment test is a clean, reusable discriminating measurement of positional/layout structure with a correct internal baseline, and the label-vs-prose comparison keyed to real locus tags is a sound framework (and, when given a size-matched null, surfaces a genuine vocabulary difference). It contributes a layout-aware structural probe distinct from the section-vocabulary scripts.
reusable_test: Stratify tokens by their real IVTFF locus/line-type tag rather than folio ranges, then compare a positional glyph distribution (e.g. line-initial vs mid-line word-initial glyphs) using the corpus itself as the baseline to detect layout-conditioned regularities; for vocabulary-overlap claims between a small line-type and a large one, require a size-matched permutation null because the open hapax-heavy lexicon makes raw novel-type fractions sample-size-driven.
confounds_ignored: Currier A/B dialect — labels/prose may segregate by dialect/section, so vocabulary novelty could track A/B not 'naming function' (confound #3)
open-lexicon/small-denominator — 54% label-novelty is reported with no null; only an external size-matched permutation (not in the script) shows it survives (confounds #2/#4)
content-free generators reproduce positional/line-initial conventions and open-lexicon novelty, so neither finding alone evidences meaning (confound #5)
adj-rep% differences are mechanically driven by line length (labels ~1 word/line) not by genuinely lower repetitiveness
key_result: Using real locus tags: prose 33629 tokens, labels 1017 tokens with 1.18 words/line vs prose 8.17; label word length (5.18) identical to prose; 54% of label vocab never appears in prose; labels start disproportionately with 'o' (52%); and line-initial words are strongly enriched for gallows/p,t and y (p x17.5, t x5.3, y x4.4) versus mid-line, while 'o' and 'c' are depleted line-initially.

purpose: Tests whether a meaningless topic-drift generator (K latent co-occurrence clusters of word-cores + affix schema + 18% copying) can match BOTH real burstiness (0.138) and hapax fraction (0.70), sweeping K to ask whether a small number of statistical topics suffices (meaningless wins) or whether ~one-topic-per-folio is needed (genuine page-specific content).
soundness_reason: The method is a legitimate generative discriminator with an explicit, falsifiable decision rule (match at small K => meaningless; need K~#folios => content), and it correctly frames the content-free generator as the null rather than treating burstiness/hapax as proof of meaning. But there is no A/B Currier split (P-lines from dialect A and B folios are pooled into one schema and one co-occurrence space), so any topic structure is confounded with the documented scribal-dialect split. More importantly the conclusion the run supports is muddied: the generator matches NEITHER target at any K (burst maxes ~0.085 vs 0.138; hapax stuck at 0.36-0.37 vs 0.70 and flat across K), so by the script's own rule neither branch fires. This particular generator is underpowered — the 18% literal-copy step plus core-pooled affix dressing collapses hapax far below the ~0.72 that other content-free generators in this session reproduce — so its failure to match is evidence about this generator's weakness, not about whether the manuscript needs page-specific content. The printed dichotomy thus oversells what a non-matching sweep can conclude.
value_reason: Contributes a reusable discriminator absent elsewhere: instead of asking whether ONE content-free generator reproduces a signature, it parameterizes generator complexity (number of latent topics K) and asks how much complexity is required to jointly match multiple signatures, with an explicit threshold (K small vs K~#folios) that maps complexity onto the meaningful-vs-meaningless question. The joint-match requirement (burst AND hapax simultaneously) is a stronger test than single-statistic matching. Underpowered as built, but the design is the contribution.
reusable_test: To distinguish meaningful page-specific content from drift, parameterize a content-free generator by its number of latent topics/states K and find the minimum K at which it jointly matches several real corpus signatures (burstiness AND open-lexicon/hapax simultaneously); if a small K suffices, simple drift explains the text, whereas requiring K on the order of the number of pages indicates genuine per-page content that simple generation cannot fake.
confounds_ignored: Currier A/B dialect not separated: cores, co-occurrence topics, and affix schema pooled across A and B folios
Latent kmeans topics over folio-distribution may themselves track the A/B split or section/illustration type rather than semantics
Generator is underpowered (literal-copy + global affix dressing collapses hapax to 0.36), so non-match is conflated with absence of meaning
No per-section or per-illustration-type breakdown; single global stream
key_result: Across K=6,20,60,150 the meaningless generator matches NEITHER target: burstiness 0.061-0.085 (real 0.138) and hapax 0.36-0.37 (real 0.70, essentially flat in K). So neither branch of the stated dichotomy is triggered; the generator simply fails to reproduce the real signatures, reflecting this generator's weakness rather than resolving the meaning question.

purpose: Tests the hypothesis that each Voynich word is a database record with three orthogonal columns (prefix=attribute | core=open key | suffix=attribute), via four sub-tests: field cardinality/closure, inter-field mutual information, positional invariants, and conserved line-width/justification.
soundness_reason: Circular and null-free throughout, and the printed conclusions contradict the script's own numbers. (A) "Closure" of prefix/suffix is manufactured: PRE/SUF are hand-curated lists of ~15-18 affixes, so small cardinality is defined in, not discovered; the 3042-distinct "open key" core is exactly the open-lexicon/productive-morphology signature a content-free generator reproduces (confounds 5,6), with no generator baseline. (B) It labels MI "low=orthogonal" but I(prefix;core)=1.33 and I(core;suffix)=1.61 bits are the largest pairs and NOT low, contradicting the orthogonality claim; no null for expected MI under a template generator. (C) The positional profile is essentially flat (len 4.9-5.5, gallows 43-57%); the only real effect is line-final shortening, the known line-edge effect, not a position-locked "column"; the invariant claim is asserted, not tested. (D) The script prints "strong negative" but corr is only -0.21, and CV(glyphs)/CV(words)=0.98 means glyphs are NOT better conserved than word count, directly refuting the "fills to a WIDTH" conclusion; the word-count/word-length anticorrelation is also a mechanical artifact of both being derived from the same line glyph total. No A/B-dialect, no I-label, no section control; P-lines only.
value_reason: Builds an elaborate "database record / justified columns" narrative on a hand-rolled affix segmentation with no null model, and its own output numbers (MI not low, CV ratio ~1, corr -0.21 mislabeled "strong") refute the claims being made. No discriminating power between meaningful structure and a content-free morphology generator; the sub-tests measure quantities that are either definitionally circular or trivially derivable.
reusable_test: Coefficient-of-variation ratio CV(glyphs-per-line)/CV(words-per-line): if line width is a conserved justification target, total glyph count should be more conserved than word count (ratio < 1). This is a clean, generic structural test (here it returns ~0.98, i.e. NO width conservation).
confounds_ignored: content-free generators reproduce open-lexicon/productive-morphology (open 'key' core)
Currier A/B dialect ignored
real IVTFF I-section labels ignored
no null/permutation baseline for MI or affix cardinality
word-length/word-count anticorrelation is a mechanical artifact of shared line-glyph total
line-final shortening is the known line-edge effect, not a positional column
key_result: Prefix/suffix show ~15-18 distinct values (because the affix lists were hand-defined) vs 3042 core values; inter-field MI is 0.20 (pre;suf), 1.33 (pre;core), 1.61 (core;suf) — the latter two NOT low; positional profile nearly flat except line-final shortening; corr(word-count, mean-word-length)=-0.21 (printed as "strong negative") and CV(glyphs)/CV(words)=0.98, both of which contradict the database-column and conserved-width conclusions the script asserts.

purpose: Tests the "manifest hypothesis": that Voynich prose is a segmentable inventory (bag of items) whose vocabulary-drift boundaries (found via TextTiling on morpheme bags) are real, more internally coherent than random cuts, align with physical paragraph marks, and reset the new-item-type accumulation.
soundness_reason: Mechanics are partly sound but two of three sub-tests are circular and confounds are ignored. (1) Coherence-vs-random: HAS a proper permutation null (500 random cuts, matched boundary count) and reports p=0.002 — but it is near-circular: TextTiling places boundaries at cosine-similarity valleys, so detected segments are coherent by the same cosine objective the test scores, while random cuts slice through coherent runs; a positive result is almost guaranteed by construction and the effect is tiny (0.686 vs 0.668). (2) Inventory-completion (new-type rate 0.294 after boundary vs 0.249 interior) has NO null/significance test and is also circular: boundaries are placed exactly where vocabulary shifts, so new-type rate must spike just after them. (3) Paragraph-alignment (42% vs analytic chance 23%) is the one genuinely sound, non-circular sub-test with a defensible baseline — and notably most boundaries do NOT align, undercutting the 'manifests = paragraphs' reading. Confounds ignored: Currier A/B dialect (114 A / 82 B folios form contiguous blocks; vocabulary-drift boundaries and segment coherence can track the A/B split rather than 'manifest' structure), and content-free reproducibility (a self-citation/char-template generator reproduces section-localization and vocabulary drift, so drift boundaries are not evidence of meaningful inventories). The docstring premise ('no word-order syntax => positional bag') is asserted, not tested here. Conclusions ('manifests open fresh item sets', 'segment identities') overreach what the tests support.
value_reason: Despite the oversold framing and two circular sub-tests, it contributes one reusable discriminating test: whether algorithmically detected vocabulary-drift boundaries coincide with the corpus's physical paragraph marks (locus '@') above an analytic chance baseline. That coupling of statistical structure to an independent physical/codicological feature is a clean, non-circular discriminator that a content-free generator need not reproduce, so it has real value even though the script's headline narrative does not.
reusable_test: Detect text-segmentation boundaries by an unsupervised vocabulary-dissimilarity method (TextTiling), then test whether they align, above an analytic/permutation chance baseline, with an INDEPENDENT physical marker (paragraph/locus marks) — coupling of statistical structure to codicology is a non-circular signal that content-free generators need not reproduce.
confounds_ignored: Currier A/B dialect blocks (coherence and drift boundaries can track contiguous A/B regions, not 'manifests')
content-free generators reproduce vocabulary drift / section-localization, so drift boundaries are not evidence of meaningful inventories
circularity: TextTiling boundaries optimize the same cosine objective the coherence test scores, and sit exactly where new-type rate must spike
untested premise that within-line shuffle implies a syntax-free 'bag'
key_result: 4116 prose lines, 308 detected boundaries (~13 lines/segment). Within-segment coherence 0.686 vs random 0.668, p=0.002 (tiny, near-circular). 42% of boundaries fall within +/-2 lines of a paragraph start vs ~23% chance. New-type rate 0.294 just after a boundary vs 0.249 interior (no null, circular). Concludes weak manifest/paragraph alignment; most boundaries do not align with paragraphs.

purpose: Claims to map the manuscript's structure on three axes: (A) how much of the corpus a hand-built prefix/suffix slot-grammar parses (residual = "edges"), (B) which contextual variable (register/line-position/section/stem) most collapses prefix entropy ("where the hinge lives"), and (C) per-folio q-onset "register score" with change-point detection to find structural "seams".
soundness_reason: Part A is descriptive but the 97% "≥1 affix" coverage is near-circular: with 21 hand-picked onsets and 17 hand-picked codas chosen to match known Voynich morphology, almost any token qualifies, so coverage measures the affix list's permissiveness, not corpus structure. Part B's clean comparison (register 1.0%, position 2.7%, section 3.1%, stem 35.6%) is the useful part and correctly shows register/position/section barely predict prefix; but the headline "stem wins / hinge lives in the stem" is largely mechanical — prefix and stem come from the SAME segmentation of the same word, so H(prefix|stem) is low partly because the segmentation already couples them, not because of an independent structural fact. Part C is the worst: the per-folio "register score" = q-onset rate is substantially a Currier A/B marker (I verified mean q-rate 0.105 for A folios vs 0.163 for B folios), so the bright block in the sparkline and the "seams" track the documented dialect split (confound #3); the change-point threshold (mean+1.2·std of diffs) has no permutation null, so "sharpest edges" are not shown to exceed chance, and many printed edges are intra-folio r/v flips within a single dialect. It also reuses the flawed folio-range section() (confound #1), though only in Part B where section is shown to be the weakest variable, limiting the damage there.
value_reason: Despite the flawed framing, Part B contributes a genuinely discriminating mechanic: a conditional-entropy comparison showing that register, line-position, and section each reduce prefix entropy by only 1-3% — i.e., prefix choice is NOT governed by these high-level contextual variables, which is a clean negative result useful for deflating "functional register" claims. The condH harness over (variable -> affix) is reusable. Parts A and C are mostly descriptive/decorative (sparkline, residual sample) and non-discriminating without a null.
reusable_test: Condition affix-slot choice on candidate structural variables (register, line-position, section, dialect) via H(slot|variable) vs H(slot), and treat a small entropy reduction as evidence that the variable does NOT control the slot; require a permutation/shuffle null before reading any per-folio rate change-point as a structural "seam," and check whether the rate simply tracks Currier A/B.
confounds_ignored: Currier A/B dialect: the q-onset 'register score' in Part C is mostly an A/B marker (0.105 vs 0.163), so seams track the documented scribal split
No permutation/null for change-point detection in Part C (threshold is arbitrary mean+1.2 std)
Part B 'stem wins' is partly an artifact of segmenting prefix and stem from the same word
Folio-range section() mismatches real IVTFF 'I' labels (used in Part B)
Affix-coverage in Part A is circular given hand-tuned, permissive affix lists; no content-free generator baseline for what coverage a random productive morphology would yield
key_result: Slot grammar parses 97.1% of tokens with ≥1 affix (61.1% full prefix+core+suffix), 2.9% residual. Prefix entropy H=3.92 bits is reduced only 1.0% by register, 2.7% by line-position, 3.1% by section, but 35.6% by the stem. Part C prints q-onset "edges" across 206 folios; the high-q block coincides with the Currier-B region, and printed edges are largely intra-dialect (A->A, B->B) with no significance test.

purpose: Tests whether the Voynich's high-frequency "glue" tokens organize around line/page layout rather than grammar: whether glue is edge-loaded, whether line edges are a specialized word distribution beyond a within-line shuffle, whether lines have a fixed positional template, and whether lines fill to a regular length ("justification").
soundness_reason: Test 2 is methodologically sound: it compares the KL divergence of line-first/line-last word distributions against the interior using a proper within-line permutation null (preserves line membership and word multiset), and real (6.82/6.51 bits) far exceeds shuffled (3.70/3.80), correctly demonstrating the documented line-initial/line-final positional effect. But the surrounding tests are flawed or oversold: Test 1's own numbers REFUTE its stated hypothesis — glue is DEPLETED at edges (first 15.1%, last 17.7%) vs interior 27.9%, so "glue frames the line / is edge-loaded" is contradicted by the data yet the framing persists. Test 3 finds NO template (every slot 71-79% content, no glue word >2%), a null result presented as if it characterized a "form/grid." Test 4 declares CV~0.31 "low" and equals it to "justified to the page margin" with no baseline, no random-length null, and ignoring that the established content-free generators already reproduce line-length regularity and line structure (confound 5). The layout interpretation is not discriminated from a content-free morphology generator that also yields line-edge specialization.
value_reason: Despite the oversold narrative around it, Test 2 contributes a clean, reusable discriminating instrument: quantify how much line-edge word distributions differ from interior, with a within-line shuffle as the null. That isolates a real, control-backed structural property (positional specialization) and cleanly separates genuine line-edge structure from an arbitrary cut. Tests 1, 3, 4 are non-discriminating decoration (and partly self-refuting), but the package as a whole still adds a sound positional-specialization test not reducible to size/dialect.
reusable_test: To test whether a structural boundary (e.g. line edge) carries position-specific lexical preference rather than being an arbitrary cut, compute KL divergence of the boundary-position word distribution against the interior distribution, and compare it to the same quantity under a within-unit permutation null that preserves unit membership and word multiset; an excess over the shuffled baseline demonstrates genuine positional specialization.
confounds_ignored: Content-free generator reproducibility: line-edge specialization, line-length regularity, and the 25% glue coverage are all reproducible by a productive content-free morphology/template generator (confound 5), so none of these support 'meaning' or 'layout function' over a null generator

Currier A/B dialect not controlled: line-initial specialists (daiin/saiin/dain vs B-dialect forms) and edge distributions may track the A/B scribal split rather than universal layout structure (confound 3)
No baseline for Test 4's 'low CV' justification claim — CV~0.31 is asserted low with no comparison to random-length text or known justified/unjustified manuscripts
Hand/scribe (meta 'H') and section/illustration type (meta 'I') not controlled; line-length and edge effects may vary by hand/section
key_result: Glue (top-30 words, 25% of tokens) is DEPLETED at line edges (first 15.1%, last 17.7%) vs interior 27.9%, refuting the edge-loading hypothesis. Line edges ARE specialized: first/last vs interior KL = 6.82/6.51 bits real vs 3.70/3.80 shuffled (proper within-line null), confirming a real line-initial/final effect. No internal template (all slots 71-79% content). Lines have words/line mean 8.4 CV 0.32 and glyphs/line mean 44 CV 0.31, which the script labels "justified" without justification.

purpose: Tests whether the first word of a folio's paragraph body ("opener") is a special index entry that predicts the page's section/picture-type better than a random word from the same page would.
soundness_reason: The core mechanic is genuinely good: it uses a within-folio control (opener vs a random word drawn from the SAME folio, averaged over 30/5 draws), which is exactly the right null to separate "opener is a special index" from "the opener just carries the page's shared vocabulary/dialect." That control directly addresses confound #3-style leakage. BUT (1) it defines sections by hand-rolled folio-number ranges (section(): n<=66 herbal, etc.) instead of the real IVTFF 'I' labels present in corpus.json meta — confound #1, the ranges are known to mismatch the real labels (it gets herbal=116 by range). (2) Its own conclusion is not supported by its own numbers: LOO nearest-centroid accuracy is 36% (opener) vs 24% (random), but BOTH fall well BELOW the 56% majority baseline, so even the "winning" opener predictor is worse than always-guessing-herbal — the classifier carries no usable section signal. (3) The MI panel is internally contradictory (suffix ratio 1.40 favors opener, but prefix 0.44 strongly favors the random word, first 0.98, len 0.90), so there is no consistent "opener is special" signal; the printed verdict "opener >> random => special index" cherry-picks. (4) It never checks whether any apparent opener>random gap tracks Currier A/B dialect rather than section (confound #3).
value_reason: Despite the oversold/unsupported printed conclusion, the within-folio control design is a reusable, discriminating test: comparing a candidate "structural" token against a random token drawn from the same page is the correct way to strip out page-level vocabulary/dialect confounds, and the LOO nearest-centroid + majority-baseline framing is the right scaffold. Run correctly it actually delivers a (negative) discriminating answer — the opener is NOT a special index — which is informative.
reusable_test: To test whether a positionally-privileged token (e.g. line/page opener) carries special information beyond generic page vocabulary, predict the target label from that token and compare against the SAME prediction using a random token drawn from the same page, AND against the majority-class baseline; only an opener that beats both the within-page random control and the trivial baseline is "special."
confounds_ignored: Uses hand-rolled folio-number ranges for sections instead of the real IVTFF 'I' labels in corpus.json meta (sections known to mismatch)
Never controls for Currier A/B dialect, so any opener-section association could track the documented A/B split rather than content/function
Printed verdict ignores that both predictors score below the majority baseline, i.e. the classifier has no real section signal at all
key_result: opener LOO accuracy 36% vs random-word 24%, but both below the 56% majority baseline; MI ratios are mixed (suffix 1.40 favors opener, prefix 0.44 favors random); ordinal corr(folio-order, opener-length)=+0.03. Net: the opener is NOT demonstrably a special index — contradicting the script's own printed conclusion.

purpose: Tests whether Voynich affixes form a functional "grammar" by checking three claims: (H1) the q- onset is a separable/productive register toggle bolted onto shared stems, (H2) prefix and suffix slots co-vary into "affix agreement" via mutual information, and (H3) the q-hinge is conditioned by line position ("page geometry").
soundness_reason: H1's core strippability test HAS a proper null: 54% of q-words have an attested q-stripped twin vs a 37% baseline from stripping the first glyph of non-q words — a real, control-anchored effect. But the rest is flawed. The "qW in prose 98% / W in labels 29%" claim is a section-size artifact (confound #2/#3): prose is nearly the whole corpus so almost any word appears in prose, and labels are a tiny set so almost any word is absent from them — there is no base-rate control, so this is not evidence of a register marker. H2 calls MI=0.186 bits "affix AGREEMENT" but that is only 6% of suffix entropy (very weak), the per-prefix top suffixes are nearly identical (Ø/dy/y everywhere, i.e. prefix barely conditions suffix), and there is NO permutation/shuffle null to correct MI's known positive small-sample bias — so the "grammar" conclusion is unsupported. H3 is descriptive counts with no significance test and no content-free control; positional onset rates are exactly what a productive content-free affix generator reproduces (confound #5). Decisively, none of the three tests distinguishes meaningful grammar from content-free morphology — separable onsets, weak prefix-suffix MI, and positional onset rates all fall out of content-free templated word generation (confounds #5/#6), yet every result is narrated as "function/grammar/hinge." Hand-rolled PRE/SUF lists also bias the decomposition.
value_reason: Despite the oversold "grammar" framing, H1 contributes one genuinely reusable and properly-nulled measurement: a strippability test (does removing a candidate affix leave an attested form?) benchmarked against a strip-arbitrary-glyph baseline. The 54%-vs-37% gap is a clean, control-anchored statistic about q-'s separability. H2/H3 as run are flourish (no nulls, oversold), but the H1 mechanic is a discriminating tool worth reusing.
reusable_test: To test whether a candidate prefix is a genuinely separable/productive morpheme, measure the fraction of words bearing it whose prefix-stripped remainder is also an attested word-type, and compare it against a baseline of stripping an arbitrary leading glyph from words lacking that prefix; a separable affix shows a significantly elevated strippability rate over baseline.
confounds_ignored: section/register size: prose vs label twin-pair rates are driven by prose dominating the corpus and labels being a tiny set, with no base-rate control (confound 2/3)
no permutation null for the prefix-suffix mutual information, which has positive small-sample bias, so 0.186 bits is uninterpretable
content-free reproducibility: separable onsets, weak affix MI, and positional onset rates are all reproduced by content-free templated morphology, yet are read as 'grammar/function' (confound 5/6)
Currier A/B dialect is not controlled; prose/label and positional effects may track the documented scribal/dialect split
hand-rolled PRE/SUF affix inventories bias the decomposition rather than learning segmentation from data
key_result: q-strippability 54% vs 37% baseline (real, nulled); q is a bound qo- onset; qW/W twin pairs occur in prose 98% / labels 29% (uncontrolled, size artifact); prefix-suffix MI = 0.186 bits = only 6% of suffix entropy (weak, no null); per-prefix suffixes nearly identical; q-onset 12.6% line-initial vs 17.3% mid vs 8.4% line-final, with ch/sh swinging far more (9.2%->32% mid). Concludes affixes are a functional "grammar/hinge," which the tests do not support over a content-free alternative.

purpose: Tests whether the picture predicts the text on the same herbal folio: do visually-similar plant pages (by crude RGB pigment proxy) carry more-similar text (vocab Jaccard) than random folio pairs, via a Mantel permutation test.
soundness_reason: The headline conclusion is backwards. The Mantel test reports r=+0.0492 (p=0.0055), but the script's own annotation states "negative = closer-looking => more shared words." A POSITIVE r therefore means visually-similar pages share FEWER words — the sim/diff Jaccard ratio is 0.974 (below 1), confirming this. Yet it prints "SIGNAL: imagery tracks text" purely on p<0.05, ignoring the sign. The actual cross-modal coupling is null-to-slightly-negative, not the claimed positive coupling. The permutation null is appropriate for testing presence of correlation, but the effect is trivially small and in the opposite direction to the stated hypothesis. Confounds: the 80 folios mix Currier A (60) and B (20); same-Currier pairs have Jaccard 0.072 vs 0.044 cross-Currier, so vocabulary overlap is dominated by the documented A/B dialect split, which color may weakly track. Vocab-size also drives Jaccard (r=0.081) while anti-correlating with visual distance (r=-0.179), so the tiny signal is partly a size artifact. Color (green/red/blue means) is acknowledged as a crude proxy and folio-to-page alignment is approximate.
value_reason: The Mantel-permutation cross-modal coupling test is in principle a reusable discriminating idea, but as implemented it is non-discriminating decoration: the effect is essentially zero (ratio 0.974) and the verdict logic ignores correlation sign, so it would print "SIGNAL" for a backwards result. It does not control for Currier A/B or vocab-size, both of which drive the residual. The descriptive suffix/color table at the end is purely narrative flourish. It contributes no clean measurement of real text-image structure.
reusable_test: A Mantel/permutation test correlating a between-item visual-feature distance matrix against a between-item text-similarity (Jaccard) matrix can probe cross-modal coupling — but only if the verdict checks the SIGN of the correlation against the hypothesis, and partials out dialect (Currier A/B) and vocab-size as covariates (e.g. restrict to within-dialect pairs, or use partial Mantel).
confounds_ignored: Currier A/B dialect split drives vocabulary overlap (same-Currier Jaccard 0.072 vs 0.044 cross), not imagery
vocab-size artifact: larger-vocab pairs have higher Jaccard and lower visual distance, manufacturing spurious correlation
correlation SIGN ignored: positive r reported as 'imagery tracks text' despite annotation saying negative is the predicted direction
approximate folio->PDF page alignment and crude RGB color proxy acknowledged but not propagated into uncertainty
key_result: 80 aligned herbal folios. Visually-similar plants share Jaccard 0.0613 vs visually-different 0.0630 (ratio 0.974 — similar plants share slightly FEWER words). Mantel r=+0.0492, p=0.0055, which by the script's own annotation means closer-looking => fewer shared words, yet it prints "SIGNAL: imagery tracks text." Effect is trivially small and opposite in sign to the stated hypothesis; same-Currier pairs dominate vocab overlap.

purpose: Tests whether Voynich labels (L-locus) and prose (P-locus) are two registers of one generator by decomposing words into prefix+core+suffix and checking (1) shared core inventory, (2) differing affix weighting, (3) labels = prose stems re-dressed, (4) labels tied to their own folio's prose.
soundness_reason: The morphology is a hand-rolled, arbitrary affix list (PREFIXES/SUFFIXES) with a greedy longest-match peel, so "core" is an artifact of the chosen lists, not a derived segmentation. Sections 1-3 (substrate/register/operator) have NO null model: with 33,133 prose tokens vs 941 label tokens and a productive affix grammar, almost any short core will appear in the much larger prose pool by chance, so the headline "78.6% label-core tokens also in prose" and "73% re-dressed" are uninterpretable without a shuffled/content-free baseline — exactly the kind of overlap that confound #5 (content-free generators reproduce productive morphology and shared cores) predicts trivially. The conclusion "labels are a derivational register of the prose lexicon" overreaches its evidence. The KL affix-difference numbers in section 2 are descriptive and fine but not benchmarked. Section 4 (LOCALITY) is the redeeming part: it uses a proper paired sign-flip permutation null comparing each folio's label-cores to its OWN prose vs sampled OTHER folios' prose, which is a legitimate discriminating mechanic. But the effect is tiny (own 0.088 vs other 0.078, diff +0.010, p=0.029) and ignores Currier A/B (confound #3): same-folio prose shares the same dialect as same-folio labels, so the locality edge can be a dialect-clustering artifact rather than page-local derivation. Mixed: section 4's mechanic is valid; sections 1-3 and the overall "one generator, two registers" narrative are baseline-free and oversold.
value_reason: Section 4's paired permutation of label-core overlap with own-folio prose vs other-folio prose is a reusable, discriminating test of whether labels are page-locally tied to their accompanying text — a genuinely useful structural probe (the only one here with a control). Sections 1-3 are non-discriminating flourish (no null, reproduced by content-free morphology), but the script as a whole contributes the locality test, so net useful.
reusable_test: Pair each page's label vocabulary against (a) that same page's body text and (b) randomly sampled other pages' body text, then run a paired sign-flip permutation on the overlap difference to test whether labels are locally tied to their own page rather than to the corpus globally — controlling for dialect/section by restricting the comparison set.
confounds_ignored: section/pool size: prose pool is ~35x larger than labels, so high core-coverage and re-dressed rates are expected by chance with no shuffle null (sections 1-3)

content-free reproducibility: a productive content-free affix grammar trivially yields shared cores and differing affix weights, so substrate/register/operator results are not evidence of meaning (confound #5)
Currier A/B dialect: the locality effect in section 4 conflates 'same page' with 'same dialect', since a folio's labels and prose share its A/B assignment (confound #3)
arbitrary segmentation: hard-coded PREFIXES/SUFFIXES define the 'core', so all core-overlap statistics are sensitive to list choices with no robustness check
key_result: Reports labels and prose share a core inventory (78.6% label-core tokens appear in prose, 73% of distinct labels are 're-dressed' prose cores, only 46% verbatim), with modestly different affix weighting (prefix KL 0.62 bits), and a small but significant page-locality effect (own-prose overlap 0.088 vs other 0.078, paired permutation p=0.029); concludes labels are a page-local derivational register of the prose lexicon — but the substrate/register/operator claims lack any null and the locality effect is tiny and dialect-confounded.

purpose: Tests whether the manuscript behaves like a "roster/org-chart over time" — a persistent population of named entities (word cores) recurring across paragraph snapshots, each carrying a changing attribute (affix), via four sub-tests: A) core-set Jaccard overlap vs paragraph lag with a shuffle null, B) core recurrence distribution, C) affix variation and q-prefix drift correlation, D) prefix-layer stacking.
soundness_reason: The "cores" the test reifies as persistent named entities are degenerate fragments of a crude prefix/suffix stripper — the headline "persistent population" is ['a','e','ol','y','ch','or','ar','ee','o','s','al','l'], single letters and stubs, not entities, so the roster framing is unsupported at the unit level. Test A does include a shuffle null and shows a real adjacency effect (0.182 vs 0.138 at lag 1), but that is exactly the section/folio/Currier-dialect locality confound (#3) and is reproducible by content-free generators with section-localization (#5); the script attributes mere vocabulary autocorrelation to "persistent membership/turnover" with no within-section or within-dialect control. Test B's 72%-hapax long tail is just the open-lexicon Zipf signature (#6) relabeled as "members vs transients." Test C's own numbers (drift mean +0.013, only 16% with |corr|>0.2) are consistent with NO structured attribute drift, i.e. they fail prediction C, yet are reported neutrally; "15.9 affix-dressings" has no null. Test D is descriptive morphology with no null and no discriminating power. Conclusion (an entity roster tracked over time) vastly overreaches what the tests can support.
value_reason: Interpretive narrative dressing standard, already-explained signals (section locality, open lexicon, productive affixation) as a "roster of named entities." The one mechanic with discriminating potential — lag-Jaccard with a shuffle null (Test A) — is oversold here (locality is conflated with roster membership and the relevant section/dialect controls are absent), and the other three sub-tests are non-discriminating or self-undercutting (C actually fails). Net contribution is rhetorical, not a clean discriminating test.
reusable_test: Lag-Jaccard vocabulary overlap between sequential text units (paragraphs) compared against a paragraph-order shuffle null measures whether nearby units share more vocabulary than expected by chance (sequential locality) — but to be meaningful it must be controlled for section and Currier A/B membership (e.g. permute only within section/dialect), otherwise it just measures topical/dialect locality, not any deeper organizing principle.
confounds_ignored: section/folio locality drives adjacent-paragraph vocabulary overlap (shuffle null only rules out zero structure, not topical/dialect locality)
Currier A/B dialect split (#3) — adjacent paragraphs share dialect
open-lexicon / 72% hapax is the content-free morphology signature (#6), not evidence of 'transient members'
content-free generators with section-localization reproduce adjacency overlap (#5)
degenerate decomposition: 'cores' are single-letter/stub fragments, not entities
key_result: 259 paragraphs. A: real adjacent core-set overlap 0.182 vs shuffled 0.138 (a locality effect, attributed to roster persistence). B: 3350 cores, 191 in >=10 paragraphs, 72% hapax; top "members" are single letters/stubs. C: 15.9 affix-dressings per core, but q-attribute vs position correlation mean +0.013 with only 16% exceeding |0.2| — effectively no structured drift, undercutting prediction C. D: prefix layers 22%/57%/16%/5% for 0/1/2/3 — plain descriptive morphology.

purpose: Tests whether a frequency-rank substitution "decoder" that makes Voynich text "look a bit like Latin" actually discriminates real Voynich from meaningless gibberish — i.e., whether the classic false-solution method carries any evidentiary weight.
soundness_reason: This is a properly-controlled debunking demonstration. It scores Latin-trigram likeness against a real ceiling (Cicero self-score -1.959), a random-letter floor (-3.757), and — crucially — a content-free null: an order-2 char Markov model trained on Voynich, gibberish by construction. Real Voynich decoded (-3.524) and the null (-3.392) land in the same neighborhood near the floor, with the null actually scoring slightly HIGHER. The conclusion "looking a bit like Latin is the expected output of frequency-matching any language-shaped token stream, not evidence" is exactly what the data support. It does not confuse size/dialect/small-denominator effects, and it explicitly instantiates the content-free-generator confound (#5) as its null rather than treating a surface signature as meaning. Minor caveats (frequency-rank mapping is a strawman of sophisticated decoders; trigram metric is coarse; single Markov draw rather than a distribution of nulls) are about scope, not validity — the core comparison is fair because real and null go through the identical pipeline.
value_reason: Contributes a reusable discriminating test: pass both the real corpus and a content-free null through the same purported "decoder + target-language likeness" pipeline, and require the real corpus to beat the null. Here it fails to (null >= real), which cleanly invalidates "it comes out looking like Latin" as evidence. This is a transferable inoculation against frequency-substitution false solutions, with proper ceiling/floor/null anchoring.
reusable_test: To validate any claimed decoding/cipher, run the SAME decode-and-score-against-target-language pipeline on (a) the real corpus and (b) a content-free null (e.g. char-Markov trained on the corpus); if the null scores as high as or higher than the real text, the target-language resemblance is an artifact of frequency-matching, not evidence of decipherment. Always anchor with a real-target ceiling and a random floor.
confounds_ignored: Uses only a naive frequency-rank substitution as the 'decoder', which is a strawman; sophisticated claimed solutions use richer mappings and could in principle separate from the null differently (though the demonstration's point still stands for the frequency-trap class).
Single Markov realization rather than a distribution of null draws, so no quantified spread on the null score — the gap is read by eye, not tested for significance.
key_result: Latin-likeness (avg log-prob/trigram): real Latin -1.959 (ceiling), random letters -3.757 (floor), REAL Voynich decoded -3.524, NULL gibberish decoded -3.392. Real and null sit together near the floor (null slightly better), far below real Latin — so frequency-decoding into Latin-looking output is non-discriminating and is not evidence of meaning.

purpose: Tests whether any glyph n-gram (trigram) is over-represented in the text of folios sharing a visual plant attribute (flower colour, root type) versus another value, i.e. whether the pictures act as known-plaintext cribs revealing cipher-morphemes for those attributes.
soundness_reason: The statistical mechanic is genuinely good: it builds per-folio trigram vectors and runs a 4000-iteration label-permutation null over the SAME folios, taking the max |log2 ratio| as the family-wise test statistic. This correctly controls for group size and the chance baseline (the confound #2 size artifact is neutralized), and it honestly reports NULL when p>=0.05 (colour p=0.64; root p=0.056, also not significant). The conclusion it draws ("no substring separates the attribute better than random regrouping") is fully supported by its own null. The real weakness is upstream of the statistics: the TAGS dict (flower=red/blue, root=taproot/rhizome, etc.) is hand-fabricated, attributed to an unspecified "vision model," and is not verifiable ground truth in the corpus — so the known-plaintext is invented. A null result survives this (garbage plaintext just yields null), but a positive would have been uninterpretable. It also ignores Currier A/B (confound #3) and locus/label structure when pooling all folio words, and n=4-6 folios per group is far too small to detect anything, which the script itself admits. So the test is correctly calibrated but rests on unverified inputs.
value_reason: Unlike most scripts in this session, this contributes a genuinely reusable DISCRIMINATING template: a known-plaintext crib attack with a proper max-statistic permutation null and an honest null verdict. The pattern (pool text by an external observable attribute, search for a separating substring, test against random relabelling of the same units) is the right shape for distinguishing a real cipher from content-free text, and it could become decisive if fed real verifiable image labels and more folios. It does not oversell — it explicitly flags the small-n caveat and demands held-out validation.
reusable_test: To test whether text encodes an external observable feature, partition documents by a verifiable ground-truth attribute, find the substring/feature with the largest enrichment between groups, and compare that maximum against a permutation null that randomly relabels the same documents — a separation only counts if it beats the max-statistic null (controls group size and multiple comparisons).
confounds_ignored: Currier A/B dialect not held constant when pooling folio text
locus/label line-type structure ignored (all words pooled)
fabricated/unverifiable image tags treated as ground-truth plaintext
tiny n (4-6 folios per group) gives near-zero power
key_result: Both crib searches return NULL: flower colour red-vs-blue best separation |log2ratio|=2.77 at p=0.64; root taproot-vs-rhizome best |log2ratio|=5.83 at p=0.056 — neither beats random regrouping, so no glyph substring tracks a visual plant attribute. Verified by running (17 tagged folios, 1474 tokens).

purpose: Parses the raw IVTFF/EVA Takahashi transcription into corpus.json (per-folio lines with locus type + words, plus real IVTFF page metadata I/L/Q/H), and prints basic corpus stats (folio count, token count, legibility %, distinct types, Currier-language tally).
soundness_reason: It is a data-ingestion/ETL script, not an inferential one, so the size/dialect/small-denominator/content-free confounds do not apply. Its EVA-cleaning choices are documented and defensible: stripping comments/markers, deleting !/% null fillers, taking the first alternative of [a:b], mapping uncertain comma-space to a real space, and preserving ? to measure legibility. Crucially, it extracts the REAL header metadata ($I illustration, $L Currier language, $Q quire, $H hand) per folio rather than fabricating sections from folio-number ranges, which is exactly the correct, confound-free basis the downstream audit treats as ground truth. Verified it runs: corpus.json carries true meta (f1r I=T,L=A) and locus-tagged word lists. The only printed 'conclusions' are descriptive counts, which the test fully supports. Minor judgment calls (single-transcriber H, first-alternative of ambiguous readings, dropping non-EVA glyphs) are openly declared, not hidden.
value_reason: It is the canonical, reusable corpus builder that every other script depends on; correctly surfacing the genuine IVTFF I/L/Q/H metadata is what makes it possible to replace flawed folio-range section reconstructions with real labels and to control for Currier A/B dialect. The legibility metric (preserving ?) is a clean, reusable measurement. Not a rhetorical flourish.
reusable_test: Ground-truth ingestion: parse real IVTFF page headers to attach authentic illustration-type (I), Currier-language (L), quire (Q), and hand (H) labels to each folio, and tag every line by its locus type (P body vs L label etc.), so downstream analyses key on documented metadata rather than reconstructed folio-number ranges; also a token legibility rate via retained '?' glyphs.
key_result: Parses the Takahashi (;H) transcription into corpus.json with {meta, folios}: ~225 folios with text, real per-folio metadata (e.g. f1r I=T Q=A P=A L=A H=1), locus-tagged word lists, and printed descriptive stats (total tokens, fully-legible % computed via tokens lacking '?', distinct legible types, and a Currier-language folio tally). Purely descriptive output; no meaning/section claims made.

purpose: Tests whether Voynich labels (locus L) behave like a hash/naming function — near-unique per object (Test 1: label unique-word fraction vs size-matched prose) and deterministic in landing in visually-consistent page contexts (Test 2: within-label spread of page color features vs random regrouping).
soundness_reason: Test 1's mechanic is fine (proper 2000-draw size-matched permutation null, p=0.0005, labels uniq-frac 0.849 vs prose 0.763), but the conclusion overreaches and ignores confounds. The prose null is drawn from the GLOBAL prose pool, while labels are not a random sample of pages: label-bearing folios concentrate on Pharma/Zodiac/Biological/Astronomical pages and a different Currier A/B mix than the herbal-dominated prose, so higher label uniqueness can reflect section/dialect register plus the fact that labels are short isolated one-per-object tokens, not a 'hash/naming code'. The result is also fully consistent with the script's own 'INDEPENDENT/filler' hypothesis (and with a content-free generator that produces isolated label tokens), so it cannot support the headline 'hash/naming' interpretation — it only excludes heavy descriptive-vocab reuse. Test 2 is degenerate and worthless: it relies on a hand-rolled recto_page folio-number arithmetic guess and discards everything past folio 57, leaving only 6 'testable' labels that are all single Latin key-column characters ('o','y','e','k','s','p') ALL on the same folio f49v mapping to the same page, so observed spread and null are both identically 0.0000 and p=1.0 is no-data, not 'no signal' — yet the script prints a substantive negative conclusion.
value_reason: Test 2 contributes nothing (6 identical-page single-char tokens, degenerate null). Test 1's permutation mechanic is reusable in principle, but as deployed it is non-discriminating: high label uniqueness is predicted equally by hashes, filler, and content-free generators, and the global-pool null fails to control for the section/dialect provenance of label pages, so it cannot separate meaningful naming from artifact. The framing (hash/naming vs descriptive vs filler) is interpretive narrative the test cannot adjudicate.
reusable_test: Comparing the type/token uniqueness of an isolated-token class (labels) against a size-matched permutation null from another text class — but to be discriminating the null must be drawn from the SAME pages/section/dialect as the target class, and high uniqueness must be checked against a content-free isolated-token generator since uniqueness alone does not distinguish naming from filler.
confounds_ignored: Section/illustration-type provenance: label pages skew Pharma/Zodiac/Bio/Astro vs herbal-dominated prose, null drawn from global prose not matched pages
Currier A/B dialect mix differs between label folios and the prose pool
Content-free generator reproduces label/body repetition split, so high label uniqueness is not evidence of meaningful naming
Test 2 alignment uses hand-rolled folio-number arithmetic (recto_page) instead of real IVTFF page metadata and discards all non-herbal pages where labels actually concentrate
Test 2 degenerate sample: all 6 testable labels are single key-column characters on one folio, giving identical vectors and a structurally-zero null
key_result: Test 1: labels uniq-frac 0.849 vs prose 0.763 (95% 0.736-0.790), p=0.0005 — printed as 'labels SIGNIFICANTLY more collision-resistant'. Test 2: only 6 aligned repeated labels, all single chars on f49v/page 97; observed spread 0.0000, null 0.0000, p=1.0 — printed as 'no visual consistency', which is actually a no-data degeneracy.

purpose: Tests whether Voynichese morphology is discoverable without hand-fed affix lists, by running two parameter-light unsupervised segmenters (Harris branching entropy + BPE) and checking whether they rediscover the hand-built slot grammar (qo-, ch-, sh-, -dy, -aiin, etc.) and how large the unsegmentable residual is.
soundness_reason: The mechanics are legitimate and standard (Harris branching-entropy boundary detection over frequency-weighted vocab; greedy BPE merges), take zero linguistic input, and are run on the whole token stream, so they avoid the section-size (#2), folio-range (#1), Currier A/B (#3), and small-denominator (#4) confounds entirely. The finding that both independent methods rediscover qo/ch/sh/cth prefixes and -ar/-ol/-or/-al/-dy/-aiin suffixes is genuine and non-circular, and it cleanly validates the hand grammar rather than assuming it. The defect is confound #5/#6: a content-free self-citation + char-template generator (already shown to reproduce this corpus's productive morphology, Heaps beta ~0.83, open lexicon) would ALSO produce strong branching-entropy boundaries and recurring BPE units — productive template morphology is exactly what generates these signals. The script runs NO null/control (no segmentation of a content-free generator or shuffled baseline), so it cannot show the degree of rediscovery exceeds what meaningless-but-productive morphology yields. It is honest in scope (it claims only that morphology is discoverable and quantifies a 14.7% residual ceiling, not that the text is meaningful), so the conclusion it actually states is supported; but absent the generator null it cannot discriminate real linguistic morphology from content-free morphology, and would overreach if read as evidence of meaning.
value_reason: It contributes a reusable, non-circular discriminating mechanic: unsupervised segmentation (Harris BE / BPE) that recovers affix structure with no hand input and quantifies the unsegmentable residual. Properly paired with a content-free-generator baseline it becomes a real discriminator (does the generator's induced morphology match the corpus's?). As run it is a clean structural measurement and a valid cross-check on the hand grammar, not rhetorical decoration.
reusable_test: Run two independent zero-input unsupervised morphology inducers (Harris branching-entropy boundaries and BPE merges) on the token vocabulary; treat convergence of both on the same recurring affixes as evidence of genuine slot structure, and measure the fraction of tokens left unsegmentable as a morphological ceiling — then compare the induced affix inventory and residual against the same procedure run on a content-free generator to test whether the structure is distinctively meaningful.
confounds_ignored: content-free productive morphology (a self-citation/char-template generator reproduces strong branching-entropy boundaries and BPE units, so rediscoverable affixes are not evidence of meaning) — no generator/shuffle null is run
open-lexicon/productive-morphology reproducibility: high Heaps beta and discoverable slots are reproduced by content-free generators, so this does not distinguish language from non-language
key_result: Both unsupervised methods rediscover the hand grammar with no input: Harris BE induces prefixes ch/qo/sh/cth and suffixes in/ar/ol/al/or/am/chy/chedy; BPE yields units including ch, ok, ot, qok, qot, ol, al, sh that match hand affixes. 85.3% of tokens get an induced boundary; the residual ceiling is 710 unsegmentable types = 14.7% of tokens (onset-dominated by o-), confirming morphology is discoverable — but with no content-free baseline, this cannot distinguish meaningful from merely productive morphology.

purpose: Tests two claims: (Part 1) that Voynich words "clump" topically like real-language content words rather than spreading randomly, using burstiness B=(σ-μ)/(σ+μ) on inter-occurrence gaps versus shuffled baselines and English/Latin; (Part 2) that the manuscript is a "collection of tables" with a shared schema but divergent per-section entity domains, via prefix/suffix MI, core-word Jaccard overlap, and within/between-section folio affix distance.
soundness_reason: Sections are reconstructed from hand-rolled FOLIO-NUMBER RANGES (n<=66 herbal, etc.) while the corpus already carries the real IVTFF 'I' labels in C['meta'], which the session proved MISMATCH these ranges (confound #1) — Part 2's entire section partition is wrong. Part 1 deserves partial credit: it DOES build a global-shuffle null (B=-0.039) and a within-section shuffle (B=+0.099), which is the right control to isolate fine vs section-level clumping. But real B=+0.138 is computed on only n=463 word-types (mink=10 on a small P-only stream), the +0.138 vs +0.099 gap is never significance-tested, and the script labels B>0 as "pro-language/topical" despite confound #5 (content-free self-citation generators reproduce burstiness IoD~1.3) — so the meaning interpretation overreaches what burstiness can support. Part 2(b) reports RAW core Jaccard overlap with NO size-permutation null (confound #2) and ignores that section vocabulary tracks the documented Currier A/B split (confound #3), yet reads low overlap as "different entity domains = different tables." purpose: Tests three "unexamined structure" claims: (1) whether word ORDER carries information beyond a bag-of-words (syntax test via bigram conditional entropy vs within-line shuffle, plus a cross-word suffix->next-prefix mutual-information binding test), (2) whether zodiac medallions have ~30 labels (a "calendar/days-of-month" reading), and (3) how regular the recipe/stars paragraphs are (line counts and recurring line-openers).
soundness_reason: Part 1 is the strongest piece and is methodologically sound in design: it compares real bigram conditional entropy H(W2|W1) against a within-line shuffle that keeps the same word-bag but destroys order — a proper null. The honest negative result (order adds +0.00 bits; cross-word suffix/prefix MI only 0.125 bits) argues AGAINST syntax and does not overreach; this is anti-confound behavior. BUT the test is nearly insensitive to its target: with a ~72%-hapax open lexicon almost every bigram is unique, so H(W2|W1) is dominated by unigram structure and a within-line permutation of short (>=3-word) lines barely perturbs corpus-wide bigram counts — the +0.00 may reflect estimator saturation as much as genuine absence of order info. Parts 2 and 3 reconstruct "sections" by HAND-ROLLED FOLIO RANGES (confound #1) instead of using the available IVTFF 'I' labels; here the ranges happen to coincide (f70-73 -> mostly real Z zodiac; f103+ -> all 23 real 'S' folios), so the empirical damage is small, but the method is the flawed pattern and the script never checks. The "~30 labels = days of a month" reading is numerology (actual counts span 19-47), and "recurring entry openers" just re-reports the corpus's most frequent words (daiin, saiin) with no null — both non-discriminating.
value_reason: Part 1's word-order test (real vs within-line-shuffle bigram conditional entropy) is a genuinely reusable discriminating test that asks whether Voynich has syntax beyond a positional bag-of-words, and it reports an honest negative result that pushes against over-interpretation. That contribution is useful and rare among these scripts. Parts 2-3 are descriptive flourishes (calendar numerology, frequency listing) with no discriminating power, but the syntax probe carries the script.
reusable_test: To test for syntax/word-order information, compute bigram conditional entropy H(W_{n+1}|W_n) on real text and on a within-line permutation that preserves each line's word multiset but destroys order; near-zero difference => order carries no information beyond a positional bag-of-words. NOTE: validate sensitivity first (e.g. on known-prose control), because with a high-hapax open lexicon this estimator can saturate and read ~0 regardless.

Estimator sensitivity: high-hapax open lexicon makes bigram conditional entropy nearly insensitive, so +0.00 order-info may be saturation rather than proven absence of syntax
No positive control (e.g. known prose) to show the shuffle test CAN detect order when present
Currier A/B dialect not separated in any part
'~30 labels = days of month' has no null; counts actually range 19-47

Recipe range (23 folios, ~47 prose-lines/folio) top line-openers are the corpus's commonest words: daiin (44), saiin (25), sain (22), dain (20).

purpose: Tests where Voynichese statistically resembles natural language vs. violates it, by running an identical metric battery (char entropy h1/h2, Zipf slope, word-length dispersion, hapax fraction, adjacent-repeat rate) on Voynich, Latin (Cicero), and English (KJV), plus splitting Voynich by Currier A/B dialect.
soundness_reason: Core mechanics are clean: it runs the SAME pipeline on real NL baselines (Latin, English), uses the REAL Currier 'L' metadata for the A/B split (not hand-rolled folio ranges — avoids confound #1), and the adjacent-repeat metric carries a built-in shuffle null that correctly distinguishes positional repetition from chance. Many of its results actively cut against "it's language" (Voynich h2=6.0 << Latin 7.4 / Eng 7.1 = more rigid; var/mean=0.68 unnaturally uniform; Zipf -0.875 vs English -1.52), so it is not naively pro-meaning. The flaws: (a) the shuffle null only rules out POSITIONAL artifact, not a content-free self-citation generator — yet the inline comment frames "real>>shuffled" repetition as evidence of structure, which content-free generators reproduce (confound #5); (b) hapax (0.709) is reported with no content-free-morphology null (confound #6); (c) token counts are not matched (Voynich 37k vs English capped at 200k), and h1/h2/Zipf/hapax are all sample-size sensitive, so the cross-corpus magnitudes are partly confounded by length and alphabet size (Voynich 22 vs Latin/Eng 26). A/B section is purely descriptive and sound.
value_reason: Contributes a genuinely reusable discriminating battery: identical-pipeline NL baselines plus a shuffle null for repetition, and several metrics (conditional entropy h2, word-length var/mean dispersion, Zipf slope) that cleanly show Voynich DIVERGING from natural language rather than matching it. These are size-sensitive but directionally informative discriminators, and the real-metadata A/B split is the correct way to handle dialect (confound #3). It would be more useful if token counts were matched and a content-free generator were added as a column.
reusable_test: Run an identical metric pipeline (conditional char entropy h2, word-length variance/mean dispersion, Zipf slope, hapax fraction, and adjacent-repeat rate with a token-shuffle null) on the target corpus AND on length-matched natural-language baselines; treat divergence in h2/dispersion/Zipf as a discriminator rather than treating any single language-like value as proof of meaning.
confounds_ignored: content-free self-citation generator reproduces the >>shuffled adjacent-repeat rate, so the shuffle null is insufficient to call repetition meaningful (confound #5)
open lexicon / high hapax reported without a content-free productive-morphology null (confound #6)
token counts not matched across corpora (Voynich ~37k vs English capped 200k); h1/h2/Zipf/hapax are sample-size and alphabet-size sensitive
key_result: Voynich looks MORE rigid than natural language on several axes: conditional entropy h2=6.02 bits (vs Latin 7.41, English 7.12), word-length var/mean=0.68 (unnaturally uniform vs ~1), Zipf slope -0.875 (English -1.52), hapax 0.709. Adjacent-repeat 0.81% >> shuffled 0.29% (positional, not chance). Currier A and B share only 14.5% of vocab (1,097 types) with disjoint signature words (A: cth*-/cho*; B: *edy/qok*), confirming the documented dialect split on real metadata.

purpose: Tests the claim that Voynich labels (locus L) are an "anti-repetitive naming regime" distinct from hyper-repetitive prose (locus P), back-computes an effective label "key-space," and flags rare-but-repeated labels as high-information "semantic collisions" / targets.
soundness_reason: Section 2 (key-space) is the sound core: it size-matches prose to the label token count via a 500-draw permutation, and the label effect survives (labels simpson_eff=418 vs prose@n 207-271 band; reprate 0.15 vs 0.21-0.27 band; keyspace ~708 vs ~315). So "labels under-repeat relative to size-matched prose" is genuinely supported. BUT three problems pull it down. (a) Section 1 presents the effect as effective-vocab RATIO (0.41 vs 0.01) comparing a 1017-token sample to a 33629-token sample — that ratio gap is a pure sample-size artifact (Simpson effective types saturate while tokens grow); the real, defensible version is only the size-matched section-2 null, which the displayed section-1 numbers misrepresent. (b) Section 3 has NO null at all: the "birthday paradox hits common words first" baseline is asserted in a comment but never computed, so labeling rare-but-repeated words as "signal/targets" is unsupported sorting, and it conflates rarity (high surprisal) with meaning — backwards in a 72%-hapax productive lexicon where rare-string collisions are expected by chance. The emitted target list is polluted with single-glyph transcription artifacts (e, p, t, x repeating x2-x3). (c) Currier dialect is ignored: labels are 188B/264A/565-unassigned tokens while prose is overwhelmingly B (22573) — the regime contrast is confounded by composition. The interpretive leap to "keyed catalog / system asserting these objects are the same / naming process" overreaches a content-free null: short single-word image-adjacent labels lacking the line-adjacent self-citation that drives prose repetition would under-repeat under any generator, so under-repetition is not evidence of semantic naming.
value_reason: Despite the oversold "naming/meaning" narrative and the uncontrolled section 3, the script contributes one genuinely reusable discriminating test: a size-matched permutation comparison of repetition/diversity (recurring-type fraction, 1/Simpson Hill number, and a birthday-estimator key-space) between two line-type populations. That test cleanly establishes labels under-repeat relative to equal-token prose, which is a real structural fact and a usable discriminator for line-type regimes. The key-space birthday estimator with a permutation baseline is the salvageable, reusable mechanic.
reusable_test: To compare repetition/diversity between two text populations of very different size, subsample the larger to the smaller's token count many times and compare the small population's metric (1/Simpson Hill number, recurring-type fraction, or birthday-paradox effective key-space n^2/2c) against the resulting null band — never compare raw per-token ratios across unequal sample sizes.
confounds_ignored: Currier A/B dialect: labels are ~half unassigned and a different A/B mix than prose (mostly B), so the regime contrast partly tracks composition not function

content-free reproducibility: short, image-adjacent, positionally isolated single-word labels would under-repeat under any generator lacking prose's line-adjacent self-citation, so under-repetition is not evidence of a semantic naming system
section 3 has no null/control for whether rare-word label collisions exceed chance; rarity is equated with information/meaning
transcription artifacts: single-glyph 'words' (e,p,t,x) are admitted as high-surprisal target collisions
key_result: Labels under-repeat relative to size-matched prose: simpson_eff 418 vs prose-at-n 207-271, recurring-type fraction 0.15 vs 0.21-0.27, effective key-space ~708 vs ~315 (this survives the permutation null). Section 1's displayed 0.41-vs-0.01 ratio is a size artifact. Section 3 emits 20 "surprising-collision" targets (incl. noise glyphs e,p,t,x) with no null, and overreaches to "system asserting equivalence / keyed catalog."

purpose: Tests whether Voynichese text is a "hash" of the page drawing (or vice versa) by checking caption-length variability, whether text length scales with drawing complexity, an information-bits budget of caption vs image, and whether the text resembles maximal-entropy hash output.
soundness_reason: The headline information-budget result rests on fabricated constants: ROOTS,LEAVES,FLOWERS,ARRANGE=6,8,4,4 are admittedly "generous counts from the sample" (invented), so the "10 image bits" and the "181x caption/image" ratio are arbitrary and not measured from anything. H_word=10.54 bits treats words as independent, ignoring the corpus's known burstiness/redundancy, badly overestimating caption bits. The "herbal" subset is selected by folio-number range (f<57), not the real IVTFF 'I' label (confound #1), and the pigment-vs-length correlation has no null and a crude "pigment area = complexity" proxy. Most importantly, none of the signals discriminate meaning from a content-free generator: a 12-15% self-citation generator reproduces the same low-entropy, self-repeating text (confound #5), so "does not look like hash output -> text is the input/meaningful side" does not follow. The directional "image = hash of text" conclusion is rhetorical, not supported by the tests.
value_reason: Largely an interpretive narrative dressed in bits. The only legitimately sound observation (Voynichese is low-entropy and self-repeating, unlike hash output) is already well-established elsewhere in the session and is non-discriminating. The CV-of-words-per-folio "fixed-length hash would be ~0" point is trivially true of any prose. The information-budget centerpiece is driven by invented numbers and an independence assumption, so it contributes no clean measurement and no discriminating test.
reusable_test: Whether text length scales with an independent measure of drawing/illustration complexity (a near-zero correlation argues against a "recipe whose length grows with what it encodes") — but to be valid it must use real IVTFF section labels and a proper null, not folio-range buckets.
